l: incursions by the barbarians of the north, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Constant attacks by barbarians of the north targeted Bin and continued despite king Tai offering valuable gifts.

l: doing good, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Mencius presents doing good as the duke’s essential business and urges him to be strong in it.

l: territory, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Tai concluded that the barbarians of the north wanted his territory. He said that a ruler should not injure his people with that wherewith he nourishes them.

l: people of Pin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people of Pin regard king Tai as benevolent and follow him in large numbers, determined not to lose him.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The kingdom is inheritance, kept from generation to generation; an individual cannot dispose of it personally and may be expected to die rather than quit it.

l: king Tai's departure from Bin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Tai left Bin after concluding northern barbarians wanted his territory, crossed mountain Liang, built a town below mount Qi, and people followed.

l: duke Ping of Lu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Duke Ping of Lu rules Lu, favors Zang Cang, and abandons visiting Meng Ke after Zang Cang questions Meng Ke’s mourning; Yue Zheng explains poverty caused the difference.

l: Zang Cang, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Zang Cang, a Zang family scion and Duke Ping of Lu’s favourite, dissuades the duke from visiting Meng Ke, preventing the visit.

l: Yue Zheng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a officer Yue Zheng questions duke Ping of Lu about not visiting Meng Ke and explains that the differences in Meng Ke’s second mourning were due to poverty and wealth. He later informs Meng Ke that Zang Cang prevented the duke’s visit.

l: second mourning, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Meng Ke’s second mourning exceeded his first in coffin, shell, grave-clothes, and shroud. Zang Cang notes the difference; Yue Zheng explains it arose from greater wealth and rites differing by status.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: This document summarizes Book II of Mencius, centered on Mencius’s account of benevolent rule, moral cultivation, and his conduct while serving and leaving Qi. Gong Sun Chou first asks whether Mencius could equal Guan Zhong and Yan in governing Qi. Mencius argues that Qi could readily attain royal dignity: its people suffer, its resources are sufficient, and benevolent government would secure genuine support. He distinguishes submission compelled by force from willing submission won by virtue, and repeatedly presents benevolence, righteousness, worthy appointments, sound policies, and care for the people as the basis of lasting rule. He identifies compassion, shame, modesty, and moral discernment as innate principles that must be developed into benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. He also praises learning from others, self-examination, and the superior man’s ability to help others practise virtue, while criticizing both narrow purity and deficient self-respect. The later chapters turn to Mencius’s actions in Qi and the objections they provoke. He maintains that offering benevolence and righteousness to a ruler is the highest form of respect, and that rulers seeking great achievements should learn from virtuous ministers. He defends accepting or refusing gifts according to their purpose, rebukes Kong Ju Xin for failing the people of Ping Lu, and explains the different responsibilities of officeholders and those without office. Incidents involving his mission to Teng, his mother’s coffin, Yan’s destruction, and the rebellion in Yan illustrate his concern for proper authority, duty, and correction of errors. Finally, Mencius leaves Qi, declining the king’s proposed house and support because it would compromise his consistency and lack of desire for riches. He explains that he had hoped to serve and reform the king, but could not remain without a proper recall or suitable treatment. His dissatisfaction comes from believing the time was ripe for tranquillity and true sovereignty, though Heaven had not yet granted the kingdom order.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius is a man and high dignitary associated with Qi who teaches and advocates benevolence, righteousness, virtue, and government directed toward the people’s happiness. He says that human accord is stronger than advantages of time or situation, that virtue wins sincere submission while force does not, and that rulers should honor virtue, employ able people, and adopt policies that gain popular support. He holds that all people have a mind unable to bear others’ suffering and should develop their human principles. He attained an unperturbed mind at forty, understands words, skillfully nourishes a vast, flowing passion-nature, and seeks to emulate Confucius rather than the narrowness of Bo Yi or the deficient self-respect of Hui of Liu Xia. In Qi he is respected by the king, yet shows greatest respect by speaking to him about the ways of Yao and Shun. He acts independently because he holds no office requiring either action or advice, although he also serves as a high dignitary and undertakes a condolence mission to Teng. His conduct distinguishes appropriate acceptance of money for travel or protection from refusal when he has no need. He buries his mother in Lu, gives up office, declines a house, allowance, and 100,000 zhong, and rejects the appearance of seeking riches or honor. Dissatisfied with Qi’s ruler but not eager to depart, he hopes daily for the king’s change of mind because the king could enable happiness for Qi and the whole kingdom. He finally leaves Qi, dwells in Xiu, and remains longer than intended when troop collection makes departure improper, maintaining that he could bring tranquillity and good order if Heaven wished it.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Gong Sun Chou is a questioner of Mencius. He asks whether Mencius could attain royal dignity through Qi and whether king Wen is the proper model; then probes the unperturbed mind, valour, will, passion-nature, words, sages, and Confucius. He also challenges Mencius’s conduct concerning illness and court attendance, and asks whether ancient officeholders served without salary.

l: Guan Zhong, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Guan Zhong is a minister who serves duke Huan, gains his prince’s full confidence, and directs government for a long time. He raises his prince to leadership over other princes and teaches the duke Huan, yet Mencius judges his accomplishments ultimately limited despite that influence.

l: Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: makes_illustrious his prince Yan is described as having made his prince illustrious. Gong Sun Chou presents Yan’s achievement alongside Guan Zhong’s as a standard for what Mencius might accomplish.

l: Zi Lu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: rejoices_when_told_about fault [when informed by another person] Zi Lu rejoiced when anyone told him that he had a fault.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: King Wen has great virtue and lives a hundred years before dying, yet his influence does not penetrate throughout the kingdom during his lifetime. Beginning with a territory of one hundred square li, he faces difficulty attaining royal dignity, but ultimately becomes sovereign of the kingdom with only a hundred li.

l: duke of Zhou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: An ancient sage who continues king Wen's course with king Wu, appoints elder brother Guan Shu to oversee Yin's heir rightly, unaware Guan Shu will rebel.

l: Wu Ding, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Wu Ding is described as a worthy, sage sovereign before Zhou, drawing princes to his court and possessing the kingdom as if moving it in his palm.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Confucius is presented as a uniquely complete Sage whose virtue spreads more swiftly than royal orders. Though called a Sage, he modestly says he learns without satiety and teaches without tiring. Mencius wishes to resemble him and affirms that none since mankind’s birth has matched him. His virtue wins the sincere submission of seventy disciples. He understands government through an ode, acts in office as proper, and teaches that virtuous manners make a neighbourhood excellent and should guide a wise person’s choice of residence.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Qi is a place with territory comparable to the royal domains of flourishing Xia, Yin, and Zhou, and people throughout the State. It needs neither more territory nor population to attain royal dignity; benevolent government could achieve it easily. Mencius lived there as a high dignitary, received no money despite a present, and was associated with advice concerning Qi Wa. Qi’s king sent Wang Huan to Teng. Mencius traveled from Qi to Lu after burying his mother, returned toward Qi, and later took leave of Qi, having remained longer than intended. Qi smote Yan, though Mencius denied advising this and said only the minister of Heaven could smite Yan. If its king used Mencius, happiness could extend from Qi to the whole kingdom.

l: the people of Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The people of Qi belong to Qi. Their sayings value favorable opportunity over wisdom and proper farming seasons over instruments, supporting the importance of timing. They approve Qi Wa’s course for Qi while questioning his own course. After Shen Tong’s question about Yan, the people of Qi smote Yan.

l: princes, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The princes appear in examples of fear, insult, and service. Sages could bring all princes to court and gain the throne without wrongdoing. Some princes sent messages and gifts to Bo Yi, who refused them; Hui of Liu Xia served an impure prince.

l: the people, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The people suffer under tyrannical government more intensely than before, admire reformed superior men of old, and revere Mencius, who says they would eagerly welcome benevolent government as relief from hunger, thirst, or hanging by the heels.

l: Yin dynasty, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The Yin dynasty retained the kingdom for a long time; its established families, old manners, and inherited influence delayed Zhou’s loss, before Guan Shu used Yin State power to rebel.

l: Zhou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: has_elapsed more than seven hundred years since its commencement [from its commencement until the present] Zhou was the place where Mencius spent the night after leaving Qi.

l: government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Government is presented as a ruler’s means of practicing benevolence and, in Qi, potentially gaining royal authority quickly. It is injured when evils of the mind are displayed in it, harming the conduct of affairs amid order or disorder. In leisure from external troubles, a prince should digest its principles and legal sanctions, demonstrating understanding of governing.

l: royal dignity, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Royal dignity is presently easy for Qi to attain, unlike for king Wen with little territory and few resources; a ruler who truly practises the five things and has no enemy in the kingdom attains it.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: makes the people [delighted] Benevolent government is presented as the action that would enable Qi’s ruler to become sovereign. Mencius says no power could prevent this result and that the people would be delighted by such government.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Virtue is an honourable quality used to practise benevolence. It enables a person to become sovereign, pleasing people and gaining sincere submission. A prince should esteem it and honour virtuous scholars. Shun treated it as common property and spread it through example. Though one of three acknowledged honors, it surpasses nobility and age in helping one’s generation and presiding over people.

l: the rise of a true sovereign, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is far removed [from the present time] The rise of a true sovereign is said never to have been more distant from the present in time, while the people’s suffering from tyranny has never been more intense. Mencius nevertheless says these conditions make the present an especially favorable time for such a sovereign to arise.

l: unperturbed mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_attainable yes The unperturbed mind is attained by Mencius at forty, while the scholar Gao attained it earlier. Mencius says that attaining it is not difficult and discusses different ways of nourishing valour in relation to it.

l: valour, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Valour is nourished by Bei Gong You through not flinching from blows, thrusts, or insults, and by Meng Shi She through rising above fear. Meng Shi She's form is inferior because Zeng attends to a more important kind.

l: the philosopher Zeng, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A philosopher who values benevolence and righteousness above wealth and nobility, sustains valour through self-examination and uprightness, and is affirmed by Mencius as expressing principle.

l: will, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The will leads the passion-nature, moving it when active alone, though the passion-nature can also move the will.

l: passion-nature, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: pervades body [and animates it] The passion-nature pervades and animates the body but is subordinate to the will. Mencius says it should be maintained without doing violence to it, and that it can be injured by trying to force its growth.

l: vast, flowing passion-nature, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The vast, flowing passion-nature is exceedingly great and strong. Nourished by rectitude and left unharmed, it fills heaven and earth, assists righteousness and reason, and arises through accumulated righteous deeds rather than incidental acts.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Righteousness is the principle of shame and dislike, requiring benevolence, wisdom, and inward complacency; accumulated through constant practice, it nourishes the vast, flowing passion-nature rather than being external or merely nourishment.

l: Song, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: In Song, Mencius was about to take a long journey and accepted a present intended for travelling expenses.

l: words, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: reveal mind [their character indicates the speaker's mental condition] Mencius says he understands words by recognizing the speaker's condition: one-sided words show a clouded mind, extravagant words a fallen and sunk mind, depraved words departure from principle, and evasive words a mind at its wit's end.

l: mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_harmed_by words [through one-sided, extravagant, depraved, or evasive speech] The mind can be unperturbed, clouded, fallen, sunk, departed from principle, or at its wit's end. Mencius says the mind should not forget its work in nourishing the passion-nature, but should not force its growth.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Bo Yi serves only a ruler he esteems and takes office under good government. He refuses unapproved or bad princes, unesteemed or bad men, and gifts that conflict with his purity; he avoids a bad prince’s court. He is described as narrow-minded.

l: Yi Yin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Yi Yin, a virtuous teacher, instructs Tang, becomes his minister, and takes office through both good government and disorder.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Shun, an emperor, delights greatly in goodness and treats virtue as shared by himself and others. From farming, pottery, and fishing through becoming emperor, he gives up his own way to follow others and continually learns from them to practise what is good.

l: ruler, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A ruler honours talented and virtuous people, employs the able, and governs markets and husbandmen with limited exactions. He levies ground-rent on shops, does not tax goods, inspects frontier-passers, and does not exact further taxes, an idler’s fine, or a hamlet’s cloth quota. By truly practising five things, he is regarded as a parent, has no enemy in the kingdom, becomes Heaven’s minister, and attains royal dignity.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Benevolence is the feeling of commiseration, Heaven-conferred dignity, and man’s quiet home. It can be practised without hindrance and brings glory to a prince; without it, propriety and righteousness are absent. It begins as either force-backed pretence or virtue-grounded practice, with virtue producing sincere submission, and ends by likening the benevolent man to an archer.

l: force, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Force pretends benevolence, subdues men, makes leaders over princes through large kingdoms, yet never wins hearts.

l: leader of the princes, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A leader of princes requires a large kingdom and uses force while pretending to be benevolent.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The kingdom is a realm of scholars, traders, travellers, husbandmen, and people won by the ruler’s policies. Its strength rests not on sharp arms but on many assisting the ruler, making it obedient to the prince. A large kingdom may lead princes through force, while virtue may make a prince sovereign. In peace it should follow clear principles and legal sanctions; commiserating government makes rule easy, and a ruler without enemies is called the minister of Heaven.

l: sovereign of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a sovereign The sovereign of the kingdom is one who uses virtue to practise benevolence. A prince need not wait for a large kingdom to become the sovereign of the kingdom.

l: a prince, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A prince who can become sovereign should hate disgrace, esteem virtue, honor scholars, appoint worthy and able people, and govern rightly so none dare insult him.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Tang, sovereign of a kingdom with only seventy li, first learned from Yi Yin, employed him as minister, and became sovereign without difficulty.

l: men, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Men submit sincerely when subdued by virtue, and their accord gives rise to a union stronger than Heaven’s opportunities or Earth’s advantages.

l: submission, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_exemplified_by seventy disciples [to Confucius] Submission caused by force is reluctant and results from insufficient strength to resist. Submission caused by virtue is heartfelt and sincere, as illustrated by the seventy disciples' submission to Confucius.

l: seventy disciples, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: submit_to Confucius [sincerely] The seventy disciples sincerely submitted to Confucius. Their submission illustrates how virtue can win heartfelt allegiance.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The Book of Poetry contains an ode and illustrates sincere submission through people of every direction accepting it. It then uses preparing a nest before rain to urge study, harmony with God’s ordinances, protection from insult, and much happiness.

l: the princes of the present day, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The princes of the present day hate disgrace yet act without benevolence, and in peaceful leisure abandon themselves to pleasure and indifference, thereby bringing calamity upon themselves.

l: people below, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_bounded_in not by the limits of dykes and borders [in accordance with these principles] A people is bounded in not by the limits of dykes and borders but by principles concerning proper rule and support.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Heaven sends calamities that may still be escaped, confers benevolence as an honourable dignity, and vouchsafes opportunities of time. It is invoked in the title “minister of Heaven” for a ruler without enemies. Heaven had not yet wished tranquillity and good order for the kingdom.

l: God, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: has ordinances of God The ordinances of God are presented as commands with which people should always strive to remain in harmony in order to obtain much happiness.

l: disgrace, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Disgrace results from acting without benevolence. A prince who hates disgrace should pursue virtue, honor virtuous scholars, and govern rightly.

l: calamity, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Calamity may result from people's own actions or Heaven; Heaven-sent calamity can be escaped, but self-caused calamity cannot.

l: happiness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Happiness is sought for itself and comes through remaining in harmony with the ordinances of God.

l: ordinances of God, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: require_harmony harmony [to obtain happiness] The Book of Poetry teaches that people should always be studious to remain in harmony with the ordinances of God, so they will obtain much happiness.

l: scholars of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Scholars of the kingdom are pleased and seek the ruler’s court when he honours talent, virtue, and able individuals.

l: market-place of his capital, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_in capital The market-place of the ruler's capital should be subject either to a ground-rent on shops without taxation of goods or to proper regulations without ground-rent. Traders will then wish to store their goods there.

l: traders of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Traders of the kingdom are pleased and want to store goods in the ruler's market-place when goods are untaxed and regulations are properly enforced without ground-rent.

l: travellers of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Travellers are pleased and wish to travel the ruler’s roads when frontier-passes inspect people without taxing goods or articles.

l: husbandmen of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Husbandmen give mutual aid to cultivate the public field; freed from other taxes, they are pleased and wish to plough in the ruler's fields.

l: people of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: People of the kingdom are pleased when shop occupiers are exempt from specified exactions and wish to become a ruler’s people when he avoids fines and cloth quotas.

l: five things, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The five things are policies concerning appointments, market charges, frontier inspections, husbandmen's mutual aid and taxes, and levies on shop occupiers. A ruler who truly practises them will have the support of the people and neighbouring kingdoms.

l: neighbouring kingdoms, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: look_up_to ruler [as a parent] The people in the neighbouring kingdoms will look up to a ruler who truly practises the five things as a parent.

l: enemy, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A ruler who has no enemy in all the kingdom is described as the minister of Heaven.

l: minister of Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The minister of Heaven is a ruler without enemies, may smite Yan, and will attain royal dignity.

l: men, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Men universally possess four principles, commiseration, shame and dislike, modesty and complaisance, and approval and disapproval, which can fully develop into virtue; helping men practise virtue marks the superior man.

l: ancient kings, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Ancient kings possessed commiserating minds and, as a matter of course, practiced commiserating government.

l: commiserating mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The commiserating mind is the inability to bear seeing the sufferings of others. When joined with commiserating government, it makes ruling the kingdom as easy as making anything go round in the palm.

l: commiserating government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: rules kingdom [with a commiserating mind] Commiserating government is practiced through a commiserating mind. It makes ruling the kingdom easy.

l: child, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A child serves as the example that reveals humanity's natural commiseration when others are in danger.

l: child about to fall into a well, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A child is about to fall into a well, prompting men who see it to feel alarm and distress without self-interest.

l: prince, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A prince gains kingdom-wide obedience with many supporters; with few, relations revolt, and fighting requires overcoming opponents.

l: feeling of commiseration, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A human feeling essential to humanity, commiseration is presented as the principle of benevolence.

l: feeling of shame and dislike, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A human feeling essential to man, shame and dislike is presented as the principle of righteousness.

l: feeling of modesty and complaisance, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A human feeling essential to man, modesty and complaisance serves as the principle of propriety.

l: feeling of approving and disapproving, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The feeling of approving and disapproving is essential to humanity and man, serving as the principle of knowledge.

l: four principles, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The four principles are present in all men like four limbs; fully developed they suffice for benevolence and to love and protect all within four seas, but if denied development they do not suffice even to serve parents.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_absent from lack of benevolence and wisdom [entire absence] Propriety is the principle represented by the feeling of modesty and complaisance.

l: knowledge, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Knowledge is the principle represented by the feeling of approving and disapproving.

l: archer, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The archer, likened to a benevolent man, adjusts himself before shooting and, when he misses, seeks the cause of failure within himself.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: bows_to speaker of good words [when hearing good words] Yu bowed to the speaker when he heard good words.

l: others, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Shun gave up his own way to follow the way of others and delighted to learn from others to practise what was good. Taking example from others to practise virtue is said to help them in the same practice.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The superior man chiefly helps men practise virtue and neither accepts bribes nor manifests narrow-mindedness or absent self-respect.

l: Hui of Liu Xia, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Hui of Liu Xia is a person portrayed as unashamed to serve an impure prince or hold inferior office. When employed he carries out his principles; when neglected or poor he neither murmurs nor grieves, remaining self-possessed because others cannot defile him.

l: office, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Hui of Liu Xia did not murmur when left without office and would remain in office when pressed to do so. He was willing to serve as an inferior officer.

l: purity, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Purity is shown through contrasting choices: Bo Yi avoids disapproved princes and their gifts, while Hui of Liu Xia remains in office when pressed, each following a different standard.

l: narrow-mindedness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius says Bo Yi was narrow-minded. The superior man will not manifest narrow-mindedness.

l: self-respect, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius says Hui of Liu Xia was wanting in self-respect. The superior man will not manifest the want of self-respect.

l: Earth, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: affords advantages of situation afforded by the Earth The Earth affords advantages of situation, but those advantages are not equal to the union arising from the accord of Men.

l: opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: An opportunity of time vouchsafed by Heaven may enable an enemy to surround and attack a city, without guaranteeing its capture.

l: advantages of situation afforded by the Earth, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Advantages of Earth’s situation provide defenses and stores, yet cannot preserve a city without union arising from the accord of Men.

l: union arising from the accord of Men, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a union The union arising from the accord of Men is presented as stronger than opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven and advantages of situation afforded by the Earth. It enables a ruler to receive broad assistance and obedience.

l: State, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_secured not by the strengths of mountains and rivers [in accordance with these principles] A State is secured not by the strengths of mountains and rivers but by principles concerning proper rule and support.

l: proper course, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Proper course brings many assistants; losing it leaves few, until even the prince’s own relations revolt.

l: king (king of Qi), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: King of Qi respects Mencius, sends a messenger and physician about his illness, gives him a present in Qi, and appoints Wang Huan assistant-commissioner. He later asks ill Mencius to come to court after the king’s cold improves.

l: Jing Chou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: advises Mencius [about respect between prince and minister] Jing Chou tells Mencius that respect governs the relationship between prince and minister and says he has seen the king respect Mencius but not how Mencius respects the king. He challenges Mencius’s failure to carry out his intended court visit after hearing the king’s order.

l: the duke Huan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: employs Guan Zhong [after first learning from him] The duke Huan first learned from Guan Zhong and then employed him as his minister, thereby becoming chief of all the princes without difficulty.

l: the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: should_enjoy tranquillity and good order [if Heaven wished this] The kingdom did not yet enjoy tranquillity and good order because Heaven did not yet wish it to do so.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: are_admirable admirable [in the judgment of the people of Qi] The people of Qi do not speak to the king about benevolence and righteousness because they believe he is not fit to be spoken with about them. Mencius says he presents the ways of Yao and Shun to the king and regards benevolence and righteousness as possessions equal to wealth and nobility.

l: respect, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a ruling principle [between prince and minister] Respect governs the relationship between prince and minister. Mencius says that speaking to the king about benevolence and righteousness demonstrates greater respect than remaining silent because the king is thought unfit to hear about them.

l: the court visit, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_governed_by propriety [according to the Book of Rites] The planned court visit is declined by Mencius when he says he is unwell. Although he later goes out to pay a visit of condolence, he is pressed to go to Jing Chou’s and spend the night there rather than immediately return home.

l: Chen Zhen, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: questioned Mencius [about gifts received in Qi, Song, and Xue] Chen Zhen asks Mencius to explain why he refused a present in Qi but accepted presents in Song and Xue.

l: Xue, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: In Xue, Mencius was apprehensive for his safety and accepted a present intended to help him procure arms.

l: present (present sent to Mencius), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A gift of 2,400 taels of fine silver is sent to Mencius in Qi, said to fund arms for protection, yet counts as a bribe if unsolicited.

l: money, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_needed_for travelling expenses [during a journey] Money was accepted by Mencius when it was needed for travelling expenses or protection, but he refused it in Qi because he had no occasion for it.

l: bribe, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a gift sent without occasion Mencius says that sending a man a gift when he has no occasion for it is to bribe him. He says a superior man should not be taken with a bribe.

l: Ping Lu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: has_governor Kong Ju Xin Ping Lu is the place where Mencius addresses its governor about failures in caring for its people.

l: Kong Ju Xin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Kong Ju Xin, governor of Ping Lu, first denies responsibility for faults among governors, then admits guilt after Mencius compares his duty to caring for livestock.

l: king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The king has cities and acknowledges guilt in a matter after hearing Mencius. He feels ashamed when thinking of Mencius, despite Chen Jia comparing him favorably with Zhou Gong. When Mencius leaves Zhou, the king does not send for him; Mencius nevertheless hopes the king will change, do good, and use him.

l: people (Ping Lu's people), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: In bad calamitous years and famine, Ping Lu's people suffer ruin: old and feeble people lie in ditches and water-channels, while able-bodied people scatter to the four quarters, together numbering several thousand.

l: bad calamitous years, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: During bad calamitous years, the old and feeble of Ping Lu's people are found lying in ditches and water-channels, and the able-bodied are scattered to the four quarters.

l: years of famine, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: During years of famine, the old and feeble of Ping Lu's people are found lying in ditches and water-channels, and the able-bodied are scattered to the four quarters.

l: Qi Wa, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Qi Wa declines Ling Qiu’s governorship for the chief criminal judgeship to voice his views, remonstrates with the king, then resigns and departs when his counsel is rejected.

l: course of action, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The course marked out for Qi Wa is viewed by the people of Qi as good, while Qi Wa’s own course is questioned.

l: giving one's opinion, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A person responsible for giving an opinion should leave when their words are not attended to. Mencius says that no duty of giving his opinion devolves on him because he holds no office.

l: Wang Huan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Wang Huan, governor of Gai and assistant-commissioner, serves the king’s condolence mission and attends Mencius throughout the journey to Teng and back.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Teng was the destination of Mencius's mission of condolence from Qi.

l: mission of condolence, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: has_destination Teng The mission of condolence went from Qi to Teng and back. Its business was attended to by proper officers rather than discussed between Mencius and Wang Huan.

l: Chong Yu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Chong Yu, a man employed by Mencius to superintend coffin-making, questions Mencius at Ying about costly wood and later, after leaving Qi, about Mencius’s dissatisfied appearance.

l: mother (Mencius's mother), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius's mother was buried in Lu by Mencius.

l: coffin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A wooden coffin for Mencius’s mother, judged too good by Chong Yu, follows a tradition of seven-inch thickness to satisfy feelings and protect the dead from earth.

l: burial of Mencius's mother, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius traveled from Qi to Lu to bury his mother, then began returning toward Qi.

l: making of the coffin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: has_object coffin Chong Yu had been employed to superintend the making of the coffin. Mencius explained that ancient practice used substantial coffin construction for everyone, from the sovereign to common people.

l: conversation about the coffin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: At Ying, Chong Yu questions Mencius about a coffin; Mencius defends it through tradition and natural feelings toward parents.

l: natural feelings, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Natural feelings favor affordable, unhindered coffin-making because it prevents earth from nearing the dead, as Mencius says traditional construction satisfies them.

l: Shen Tong, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Shen Tong asked Mencius whether Yan might be smitten. He did so on his own impulse, without the text saying that he asked who might smite it.

l: Zi Kuai, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: has_no_right_to_give Yan [to another man] Zi Kuai had no right to give Yan to another man.

l: Zi Zhi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: has_no_right_to_receive Yan [from Zi Kuai] Zi Zhi had no right to receive Yan from Zi Kuai.

l: Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Yan was treated by Mencius as a case in which Zi Kuai had no right to give it away and Zi Zhi had no right to receive it. The people of Qi smote Yan, which Mencius questioned by asking how one Yan could smite another Yan.

l: the smiting of Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_advised_by Mencius [not advised as Qi's action] The smiting of Yan followed Mencius's statement that Yan might be smitten. Mencius clarified that he would have authorized it only if carried out by the minister of Heaven, not by Qi.

l: people of Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: rebelled_against Qi The people of Yan rebelled.

l: Chen Jia, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: considers Zhou Gong [an example for comparison with the king of Qi] Chen Jia told the king of Qi not to grieve and compared the king's benevolence and wisdom with those of Zhou Gong. He then saw Mencius and questioned him about Zhou Gong and Guan Shu.

l: Guan Shu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Guan Shu, Zhou Gong’s elder brother, was appointed to oversee Yin’s heir but used Yin’s power to rebel, revealing Zhou Gong’s appointment error.

l: rebellion of the people of Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a rebellion The rebellion of the people of Yan led the king of Qi to feel ashamed when he thought of Mencius.

l: rebellion of Guan Shu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a rebellion Guan Shu rebelled with the power of the Yin State after being appointed to oversee the heir of Yin.

l: appointment of Guan Shu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a appointment Zhou Gong appointed Guan Shu to oversee the heir of Yin. Mencius said Zhou Gong did not know that Guan Shu would rebel and that the appointment was understandable because Guan Shu was his elder brother.

l: error, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_in_accordance_with what is right [the error of Zhou Gong] Mencius said that Zhou Gong's error was in accordance with what was right. He contrasted the errors of superior men of old, which they reformed, with those of present superior men, who persist in them and apologize for them.

l: reformation of errors, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a reformation Superior men of old reformed their errors. After reforming, they were again regarded by the people with their former admiration.

l: shame of the king of Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a shame The king of Qi experienced shame when he thought of Mencius because the people of Yan had rebelled.

l: the king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The king visits Mencius, regrets Mencius’s departure and uncertainty about meeting again, then proposes a house in the kingdom’s middle and support for Mencius’s disciples.

l: officer Shi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: conveys the king [through disciple Chen] The officer Shi was told by the king to convey the proposal about a house and an allowance to Mencius. He conveyed the message through the disciple Chen.

l: native State, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius arranged to return to his native State after giving up his office.

l: office, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius gave up his office and made arrangements to return to his native State.

l: riches and honour, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A topic encompassing riches and honour: Mencius says people desire them, denies seeking riches, and condemns monopolizing market advantage for gain.

l: the king's visit to Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a visit The king's visit gave him an opportunity to be by Mencius's side, which made his court rejoice. During the visit, the king expressed concern that Mencius was leaving and might not be seen again.

l: Mencius's departure from office, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius's departure from office in Qi followed his failure to find a ruler in the king who suited him. Though constrained to leave, he delayed three nights in Zhou, hoping for recall. After the king failed to send after him, he went to Cao; the king later regretted it and considered support for Mencius and his disciples.

l: Mencius's return home, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: is_a return Mencius arranged to return home after giving up his office. He said that he desired to visit the king, although he did not request permission to do so at a particular time.

l: taxing of traders, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: arises_from a conspicuous mound [through the conduct of a mean fellow] The taxing of traders was said to have begun because a mean fellow sought a conspicuous mound in the market to look over the traders and capture the whole gain. The people regarded his conduct as mean and proceeded to lay a tax on the traders' wares.

l: visitor (person who wished to detain Mencius), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: A visitor, acting for the king, anxiously plans to detain Mencius, is displeased when Mencius sleeps, then hears Mencius distinguish his treatment from Zi Si’s.

l: king (in Chong), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: The king in Chong was seen by Mencius during an interview before Mencius intended to leave.

l: duke Mou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: keeps remembrancer (by the side of duke Mou) [by his side] The duke Mou retained Zi Si by keeping a person beside him. He also needed a remembrancer beside him in order to make Xie Liu and Shen Xiang feel at home and remain with him.

l: Zi Si, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Zi Si would not have remained with the duke Mou if the duke had not kept a person by his side.

l: detaining Mencius on behalf of the king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: serves king [on behalf of the king] The visitor wished to detain Mencius on behalf of the king and approached him to discuss the matter.

l: plans concerning Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: concern Mencius [with reference to him] The visitor anxiously formed plans concerning Mencius, but Mencius said that the visitor did not treat him as the duke Mou had treated Zi Si.

l: Yin Shi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Yin Shi criticizes Mencius’s intelligence, motives, and lingering departure, but after hearing Mencius’s explanation admits he is a small man.

l: the king's change of mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Mencius continues to hope daily that the king will change. He says that if the king had changed, he would certainly have recalled him.

l: tranquillity and good order, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Tranquillity and good order were described as the condition Heaven might wish the kingdom to enjoy, and Mencius said he could bring them about if Heaven wished.

l: Xiu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Xiu was the place where Mencius dwelt after leaving Qi.

l: salary, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Salary was declined by Mencius because he intended to leave after his interview with the king in Chong. He explained that the ancients did not generally hold office without receiving it.

l: Chong, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: Chong was the place where Mencius saw the king.

l: orders for the collection of troops, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou)
s: are_issued troops Orders for the collection of troops arrived after Mencius declined salary. Their arrival made it improper for him to beg permission to leave.

l: Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: This record summarizes Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong), in which Mencius teaches rulers, scholars, and critics that humane government and moral integrity depend on following the way of the sages. It begins with the prince who becomes duke Wen of Teng: Mencius tells him that human nature is good and that even small Teng can become a good State. After Duke Ding dies, Mencius urges the prince to observe the three years’ mourning despite opposition; the prince’s sincere grief wins public admiration. As duke, he asks how to govern, and Mencius prescribes secure livelihoods, fair land arrangements, education, and benevolent rule, explaining the nine-squares system and mutual cultivation of a public field. Mencius then disputes Xu Xing’s demand that rulers farm alongside everyone else, defending a division of labor and rulers’ duty to provide order and moral instruction. He challenges the Mohist Yi Zhi for advocating spare funerals while burying his own parents richly, arguing that filial feeling naturally requires proper burial; Yi Zhi accepts the instruction. Part II develops Mencius’s defense of principle. He rejects waiting on princes merely for influence, says a great man cannot be moved by riches, poverty, or power, and explains that officers may seek office only through proper means. He defends support for scholars whose moral service benefits society. Addressing Song’s danger from Qi and Chu, he says genuine royal government would draw the people’s allegiance, as Tang and king Wu did when overthrowing oppressors. He stresses that a ruler’s attendants shape his character and that one virtuous adviser cannot reform a king surrounded by bad influences. Mencius also condemns delaying the end of known injustice, using the stolen fowls comparison. He explains that he disputes Yang Zhu, Mo Di, and other teachings because disorder follows when sage principles decline; he aims to defend the sovereign, filial affection, and the work of Yu, Zhou Gong, and Confucius. The book closes with his criticism of Chen Zhong’s supposed purity as impractical and inconsistent.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Mencius is a teacher, philosopher, and superior man in Zou who advocates benevolent government and holds principles he will not improperly bend. He teaches that human nature is good, repeatedly praises Yao and Shun, and presents Teng as capable of becoming a good State. His political teaching begins with personal example and proper filial conduct: rulers should fulfill funeral duties, seek remedies in themselves, and lead their inferiors. It develops into a program for the people’s secure livelihood, fair land arrangements, taxation and mutual aid, education, and the nine-squares system. He rejects Xu Xing’s universal self-sufficiency and market doctrine, defending exchange, specialized occupations, government, and the work of ancient sages. In correcting Yi Zhi, he argues that affection begins with parents and that burial arises from natural filial feeling. Mencius refuses to go to princes without invitation, explaining that office and support may properly be desired or received only on proper grounds, never through improper conduct. He defines a great man as one who maintains principles, serves the people when in office, and remains steady through riches, poverty, and power. He also argues that true royal government attracts people, that rulers’ attendants shape their virtue, and that recognized unrighteousness must end without delay. Although not fond of disputing, he says prevailing doctrines compel him to oppose Yang Zhu, Mo Di, and other perverse doctrines. He defends the former sages, seeks to rectify men’s hearts, and criticizes Chen Zhong for conduct inconsistent with his claimed purity.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Duke Wen of Teng is first a prince and later a duke who rules Teng. While traveling to Chu through Song, he visits Mencius twice and learns that human excellence is attainable and small Teng can become a good State. As duke, he seeks guidance on government and land division, practices benevolent government, and grants Xu Xing a dwelling-place.

l: Chu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Chu is a destination visited by the prince later duke Wen of Teng, and a hostile power that hates and attacks Song; Mencius says Song’s royal government would make Chu less fearful.

l: Song, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Song is a small State, visited by the future duke Wen of Teng while traveling to Chu to see Mencius. Its ruler is reportedly beginning true royal government, though Mencius disputes this; he says genuine practice would draw people from throughout the four seas and make Qi and Chu little threat.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Teng is a small State, about fifty li in length and breadth, yet sufficient to become good. Though narrow, it has both superior men and country-men. Mencius urges its ruler toward excellence through defined boundaries, regulated land and allowances, and mutual aid. Teng later receives Xu Xing and his disciples; its prince is praised for benevolent government.

l: human nature, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_good goodness Mencius teaches the prince, afterwards duke Wen of Teng, that human nature is good.

l: Yao, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Yao, a sage, anxiously confronts disorder from floods, vegetation, and beasts, then raises Shun to office.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Shun is a sage and exemplar of human excellence, described as a man whose stature can be reached through effort. After receiving the kingdom from Yao, he regulates disorder, appoints Xie to teach human relations, commits to Yi’s direction of fire, and anxiously seeks Yu and Gao Yao.

l: Zhou Gong, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Zhou Gong is a sage associated with ancient doctrines. He assists king Wu in destroying the tyrant Zhou, then smites Yan and executes its sovereign after three years. He drives Fei Lian to the sea and slays him, extinguishes fifty States, and removes ferocious animals from the country. His doctrines are studied by Chen Liang, and Mencius cites praise-songs describing his punishments of western and northern barbarians, Jing, and Shu.

l: the prince (successor to Duke Ding of Teng), Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The prince succeeds Duke Ding of Teng. Formerly devoted to horsemanship and sword-exercise rather than learning, he consults Mencius through Ran You after Duke Ding’s death, rejects opposition to observe three years’ mourning, dwells in a shed for five months, and exemplifies grief for officers and ministers.

l: Ran You, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Ran You twice travels to Zou to consult Mencius for the prince, then reports Mencius’s advice and commission back.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Confucius is a sage, teacher of administration, and maker of the Spring and Autumn. He praises Yao’s Heaven-corresponding virtue and Shun’s detached possession of the kingdom. He values determined and brave officers who remember possible death, and approves a forester who refuses an improper summons. He becomes anxious after three months without a ruler’s employment and carries a proper gift when crossing a State boundary. He watches for Yang Huo’s absence and pays respects after Yang Huo takes the initiative. When decay returns and principles fade, he makes the Spring and Autumn; its judgments make rebellious ministers and villainous sons afraid, making him known by it and condemning through it.

l: Zou, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Zou is the place to which Ran You travels to consult Mencius.

l: the prince's aged relatives, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: oppose three years' mourning The prince’s aged relatives oppose his decision to observe three years’ mourning. Later, they say that the prince may be understood to know the ceremonies after he has dwelt in the shed for five months.

l: the officers, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: oppose three years' mourning [as a body] The officers oppose the prince’s observance of three years’ mourning, arguing that former princes did not follow the practice. Later, they say that the prince may be understood to know the ceremonies.

l: the mass of the people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: A great man practices his principles for the good of the people when he obtains his desire for office.

l: funeral duties, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Mencius advises the prince that funeral duties to parents, like duties to aged relatives, require utmost filial piety according to propriety.

l: three years' mourning, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Three years’ mourning is equally prescribed by the three dynasties and binding from sovereign to people; Mencius says the prince resolves to observe its coarse garment and congee despite opposition.

l: the ceremonies, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Mencius says he has not learned the ceremonies observed by princes, but identifies several mourning practices as prescribed by the three dynasties. The prince’s aged relatives and officers later judge that he understands the ceremonies.

l: the death of Duke Ding of Teng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a death The death of Duke Ding of Teng causes the great duty of mourning and funeral observance to devolve upon his successor, the prince.

l: the interment, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: At the prince’s interment, people across the State and the prince’s aged relatives witness it; visitors from other States condole and are pleased by his deep, mournful grief.

l: the people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The people require a secure livelihood for a fixed heart; without it they fall into self-abandonment, moral deflection, depravity, and wild license, so they need fair treatment, education, mutual assistance, and protection from oppressive exactions.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Benevolent government, practised by duke Wen of Teng, rejects wealth-seeking and regulated taking from the people. It begins with livelihoods and land boundaries, then provides fair division, allowances, education, mutual aid, and rulers’ responsibility to govern, teach, and benefit people.

l: Zhou dynasty, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a dynasty [the dynasty of Zhou] Zhou is the dynasty whose sovereign the people of Shang said they would serve in order to be made happy. The men of station of Zhou were met by men of station of Shang bearing black and yellow silks.

l: tax system, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: A land-allocation tax system averages several years to fix a regular amount, seeming light in good years but demanding full payment in bad years, forcing borrowing.

l: system of mutual aid, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: A land-allocation system of mutual dependence, with families cultivating a public field alongside private fields; Mencius recommends reserving one division in Teng.

l: nine-squares system of dividing the land, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: requires boundaries [as its first condition] The nine-squares system divides a square li into nine squares containing nine hundred mu. The central square is public, while eight families each receive a private hundred mu and cultivate the public field together before attending to their private affairs.

l: public field, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The public field, central to nine squares, is jointly cultivated by eight families before they attend private affairs.

l: Chapter 4, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: contains Xu Xing Chapter 4 presents Xu Xing's doctrines and Mencius's arguments against them, including discussions of labor, government, ancient sages, moral instruction, and market prices.

l: Xu Xing, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Xu Xing, a person from Chu, comes to Teng, resides there, and teaches Shen Nong’s ideal of rulers farming and governing alongside their people.

l: Chen Xiang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Chen Xiang, a Song disciple and Xin’s younger brother, abandons prior learning to follow Xu Xing, then reports and defends Xu Xing’s teachings to Mencius.

l: Chen Liang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Chen Liang, a native of Chu, studies Zhou Gong and Zhong Ni in the Middle Kingdom and becomes Chen Xiang's teacher.

l: Xu Xing's doctrines, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Xu Xing's doctrines advocate rulers farming and preparing food with their people, division of labor, and equal market standards and prices to prevent deceit.

l: handicraftsmen, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: have proper_business [distinct from the business of husbandry] Handicraftsmen produce articles such as caps, boilers, pans, and iron shares, which are exchanged for grain. Mencius says their work cannot be carried on together with the work of husbandry by the same individual.

l: division of labor, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Division of labor is a universally recognised principle distinguishing handicraftsmen from husbandmen, unfolding as mental rulers and bodily workers mutually supporting and governing one another.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Yu, a sage, regulates waterways and the great inundation toward the sea and Jiang; during eight years away from home, he passes his door three times without entering.

l: moral nature, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Moral nature belongs to men and requires humane relations taught after people are fed, clothed, and housed, lest they become beastlike.

l: relations of humanity, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Relations of humanity consist of affection, righteousness, separate functions, proper order, and fidelity among five paired roles.

l: the kingdom, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The kingdom, governed by Yao and benefiting from benevolence, requires government, moral instruction, and diverse occupations to avoid confusion.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a benefit_to_the_kingdom [finding a man who shall benefit the kingdom] Benevolence is described as finding a person who will benefit the kingdom. Mencius says that giving the throne to another person is easy, while finding such a beneficial person is difficult.

l: the barbarians of the west and the north, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: are_changed_by Middle Kingdom [according to the doctrines of the great land] Mencius says he has heard of people using the doctrines of the great land to change barbarians, but not of barbarians changing others. He calls Xu Xing a shrike-tongued barbarian of the south whose doctrines differ from those of the ancient kings.

l: the Middle Kingdom, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The Middle Kingdom, once inundated and unsettled in Yao’s time, became cultivable after Yu ordered the waters; it is later associated with Chen Liang’s study of Zhou Gong and Zhong Ni and ancient kings’ doctrines changing barbarians.

l: Zhong Ni, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a sage [associated with the ancient doctrines] Zhong Ni's doctrines are studied by Chen Liang together with those of Zhou Gong in the Middle Kingdom.

l: market, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: has prices [under Xu Xing's market doctrine, no two prices] The market is presented as a place where goods of unequal quality and value are exchanged. Mencius says that making unlike goods equal in price would create confusion and encourage deceit.

l: Xu Xing's market doctrine, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Xu Xing's market doctrine claims that equal quantities, lengths, weights, or sizes of goods should have equal prices, so that no one could impose on another. Mencius rejects it because goods naturally differ in value and equal pricing would discourage the making of larger or better goods.

l: Yi Zhi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Yi Zhi, a Mohist, seeks Mencius to defend love beginning with parents, yet faces his own sumptuous burial of them despite sparse-funeral doctrine; Mencius explains, and Yi Zhi accepts instruction.

l: Xu Bi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a the learned [disciple] Xu Bi served as the intermediary through whom Yi Zhi initially sought to see Mencius.

l: Mo Di, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Mo Di advocates spare simplicity in funerals and equal love; his widely circulating words, alongside Yang Zhu’s, prompt Mencius’s opposition over filial affection.

l: Mohists, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The Mohists are associated in the discussion with the view that funeral arrangements should follow spare simplicity.

l: Mohist doctrines, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: seek_to_change the customs of the kingdom Mohist doctrines are described as teaching spare simplicity in funeral matters and as being used by Yi Zhi to seek changes in the customs of the kingdom.

l: the people, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: have_no_place_to_settle the Middle Kingdom [during the great inundation] The people suffered when floods, oppressive rulers, gardens, parks, and neglected fields deprived them of places to live, clothing, and food. They rejoiced when Zhou Gong drove away ferocious animals and restored repose.

l: the parents, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: are one root [in Heaven's ordering of creatures] The parents are the immediate object of filial affection and are to be treated with proper burial. Mencius presents the impulse to cover and inter the bodies of deceased parents as arising from natural emotional response.

l: burial of parents, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is a proper rule [when done in a handsome manner] Burial of parents is discussed as a practice that should follow a proper rule rather than spare simplicity alone. Yi Zhi's sumptuous burial of his parents conflicted with the Mohist view he supported, while Mencius defended handsome burial as consistent with filial virtue.

l: Chen Dai, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Chen Dai tells Mencius that refusing to wait upon the princes seems like standing on a small point. He argues that waiting upon them might allow one to become sovereign or chief of the other princes.

l: princes, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: are_subject_to Mencius [as rulers he refuses to follow by bending his principles] The princes are those whom Mencius refuses to wait upon without an invitation. Chen Dai suggests that waiting upon them could enable one of them to become sovereign or chief of the other princes.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: attacks Song [with hostility] Qi hates and attacks the ruler of Song. Mencius says that if Song truly practised royal government, Qi would not be much to fear.

l: principles, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Mencius says that bending his principles to follow the princes would be improper. He concludes that no one who has bent himself has ever been able to make others straight.

l: Jing Chun, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Jing Chun asks Mencius whether Gong Sun Yan and Zhang Yi are really great men. He describes their anger as frightening all the princes and their quietness as extinguishing trouble throughout the kingdom.

l: Gong Sun Yan, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_considered great man [according to Jing Chun] Gong Sun Yan is presented by Jing Chun as a man whose anger makes all the princes afraid. He is included with Zhang Yi among those whom Mencius says are not great men.

l: Zhang Yi, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_considered great man [according to Jing Chun] Zhang Yi is presented by Jing Chun as a man whose anger makes all the princes afraid. He is included with Gong Sun Yan among those whom Mencius says are not great men.

l: women, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: have_as_correct_course compliance [as a rule] Women are described through the Ritual Usages as being taught that compliance is their correct course. A young woman is cautioned to be respectful, careful, and obedient to her husband.

l: world, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The world has a wide house, correct seat, and great path, where a great man dwells, stands, and walks.

l: great man, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: A great man inhabits the world’s proper way, acts for the people when in office, and remains faithful to principle when disappointed. From public service to solitude, he resists the corrupting pull of riches and honours, poverty and mean condition, and power and force.

l: Zhou Xiao, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: asks Mencius [about whether superior men of old time took office] Zhou Xiao asks Mencius whether superior men of old time took office. He questions whether condoling with an officer after three months of unemployment showed excessive urgency and asks why a superior man might make difficulty about taking office.

l: officers, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: lose office [when they lose their place] Officers were condoled with when they had been unemployed by a ruler for three months. Their loss of office is compared to a prince's loss of his State, and their office is compared to a husbandman's plough that is carried from one State to another.

l: office, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_like plough [in an officer's situation] Office is presented as necessary for an officer's proper work, like a plough is necessary for a husbandman. The ancients desired office but did not accept obtaining it by an improper way.

l: seeking office by an improper way, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Seeking office improperly is likened to youths secretly making access to each other; ancients sought office but rejected gaining it this way.

l: Peng Geng, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Peng Geng asks Mencius whether it is extravagant for a scholar to live upon different princes while accompanied by many carriages and attendants. He argues that supporting a scholar who performs no ordinary service is improper, but accepts that remuneration is based on work done rather than intention.

l: scholar, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The scholar is described as moving between princes and receiving support despite performing no ordinary trade. A scholar who is filial at home, respectful abroad, and watches over ancient principles is presented as providing a service worthy of support.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The superior man is filial and respectful, practices benevolence, righteousness, and ancient principles, serves others and merits support, while awaiting future learners; his purpose in practicing principles is not the issue.

l: carpenters, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Carpenters are workers who seek living and obtain food through interchange by their trade.

l: carriage-wrights, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Carriage-wrights seek living through trade, exchanging work for food; Peng Geng contrasts this with the superior man's principles.

l: intercommunication of the productions of labour, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Intercommunication enables people to exchange surplus products of labour, so one person’s overplus supplies another’s deficiency.

l: interchange of men's services, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: is_a interchange The interchange of men's services allows one person's overplus to supply another person's deficiency. Through it, workers such as carpenters and carriage-wrights can receive food from others.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Benevolence and righteousness are principles practiced by filial, respectful scholars who preserve ancient teachings. Mencius sees this practice as worthy of support; unless Confucius’s principles are proclaimed, perverse doctrines obstruct their path and lead toward mutual human destruction.

l: support, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Support should be given when there is a proper ground for receiving it. Mencius argues that a scholar who serves society through virtuous conduct deserves support, just as workers receive support through exchanged labor.

l: service, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: deserves support [when it is useful to someone] Service, rather than intention, is what Mencius says should be remunerated. The example of a person who damages tiles and walls shows that an intention to earn a living does not justify payment without useful work done.

l: Wan Zhang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: asks Mencius [about Song's situation] Wan Zhang asks Mencius what should be done because Song is small and Qi and Chu hate and attack its ruler.

l: true royal government, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: makes the four seas [if genuinely practised] True royal government is presented as a rule that wins the longing and support of people throughout the four seas. Mencius says its practice would cause people to look for the ruler as their sovereign.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Tang, dwelling in Bo, aids Ge with sacrificial animals and cultivators; after Ge’s chief has provision-carriers robbed and killed, Tang punishes him, consoles people, and gains their support through his campaigns.

l: State of Ge, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: has_ruler chief of Ge The State of Ge adjoined the place where Tang dwelt in Bo. Its chief neglected sacrifices, and Tang later punished the State of Ge after its people attacked provision-carriers.

l: chief of Ge, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: The chief of Ge is a ruler whose dissolute conduct includes neglecting sacrifices, consuming sacrificial oxen and sheep, and intercepting provision-carriers for wine, rice, millet, and paddy. His people rob Tang’s labourers; after a boy carrying millet and flesh is killed and robbed, Tang punishes him.

l: Tang's punishment of Ge, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Tang’s first punitive act began with the State of Ge, punishing its chief for murdering and robbing a boy carrying food; people praised vengeance for common people over wealth.

l: the four seas, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: supports Tang's punishment of Ge [as vengeance for a common man and woman] All within the four seas supported Tang’s punishment of Ge and longed for Tang like people longing for rain during severe drought. Mencius says that if Song truly practised royal government, all within the four seas would seek its ruler.

l: Tang's punitive expeditions, Mencius, Book III (Teng Wen Gong)
s: Tang made eleven punitive expeditions, gaining no enemies in the kingdom as regions eagerly awaited his arrival.
